items.title: Our story
items.seoDescription: How a home baker’s starter became a bakery and café on Quay Street.

blocks.headline: It started with one jar of starter
blocks.body: Fifteen years, four ovens and a great many loaves later, the starter is still alive and still fed every morning.

image.alt: Hands kneading dough on a floured table

blocks.heading: From a home kitchen to Quay Street
blocks.html:
Kettle & Crumb began in 2009 as a Saturday stall: forty loaves, a borrowed table and a queue that grew every week. Within two years we had a small shop on Quay Street, and a bakery behind it with a stone-floored oven we still use today.

We bake the way bread used to be made. Our doughs ferment slowly, for up to forty-eight hours, which gives them their flavour and makes them easier to digest. We buy our flour from a mill an hour away and our butter from a dairy along the coast.

What we believe

  • Time is an ingredient. Nothing is rushed.
  • Local where we can. Flour, butter, eggs and fruit from nearby farms.
  • Nothing goes to waste. Yesterday’s bread becomes today’s croutons, puddings and toast.

blocks.heading: The night shift
blocks.body: Our bakers start at 4am so the shelves are full by 7. If you walk past early, knock on the window: there is usually something warm to try.

items.title: Why our sourdough takes two days
items.seoDescription: A long, cold fermentation is the secret behind our country loaf. Here is what happens in those 48 hours.

blocks.headline: Why our sourdough takes two days

image.alt: A sourdough loaf cut open to show its crumb

blocks.html:
People often ask why a loaf of ours costs more than one from the supermarket. The honest answer is time. Every country loaf spends two days with us before it reaches the shelf.

Day one: the mix

We feed our starter in the morning and mix the dough in the afternoon: flour, water, salt and starter, nothing else. Then it rests in the cool of the bakery overnight, slowly fermenting.

Day two: shape and bake

At 4am the dough is shaped by hand and baked in a stone-floored oven at 250°C. The long rest gives the crust its colour and the crumb its gentle tang.

Slow bread is easier to digest and stays fresh for days.

Try a loaf on a Tuesday and it will still make perfect toast on Saturday.

items.title: Meet the night shift
items.seoDescription: While the town sleeps, three bakers fill our shelves. Meet Tom, Ines and Sami.

blocks.html:
Most of our customers never meet the people who bake their bread. They start work at 4am, finish just after lunch and are usually asleep by the time the café is busiest.

  • Tom has been with us since the market stall and still shapes every rye loaf by hand.
  • Ines runs pastry. Her croissants take three days and she will not hurry them.
  • Sami joined as an apprentice last year and now bakes our weekend cardamom buns.

If you are passing early, wave through the window. They will wave back.

blocks.headline: Autumn on the counter
blocks.body: New this month: spiced buns, pear and almond tarts, and a dark loaf with toasted seeds.

blocks.html:
As the mornings get colder we bake a little richer. Look out for pear and almond tarts on Fridays, cinnamon and cardamom buns at the weekend, and a new loaf with toasted sunflower and pumpkin seeds every day.

Our pumpkin soup is back in the café from noon, served with a thick slice of country sourdough.

items.title: Seeded rye at home
items.seoDescription: Our seeded rye, scaled down for a home oven. One loaf, three days, very little work.

blocks.headline: Seeded rye at home
blocks.body: Dense, dark and full of seeds. Most of the time is waiting.

image.alt: Slices of seeded rye bread on a wooden board

blocks.heading: Ingredients
blocks.html:
• 300 g wholemeal rye flour
  • 100 g active rye starter
  • 350 g warm water
  • 150 g mixed seeds (sunflower, pumpkin, linseed), soaked overnight
  • 9 g salt
  • 1 tbsp dark treacle

blocks.heading: Method
blocks.html:
1. Day one: mix everything into a thick, sticky paste. Cover and leave at room temperature for 12 hours.
  2. Day two: scrape into a greased loaf tin, smooth the top and leave to rise by about a third, 3 to 4 hours.
  3. Bake at 220°C for 15 minutes, then 190°C for 50 minutes.
  4. Day three: wait a full day before slicing. Rye needs time to set.

items.title: Butter croissants
items.seoDescription: Laminated dough, cold butter and patience: how we make our croissants.

blocks.headline: Butter croissants
blocks.body: Not quick, but not hard either. Keep everything cold and do not rush the folds.

image.alt: Rows of golden croissants on baking paper

blocks.heading: Ingredients
blocks.html:
• 500 g strong white flour
  • 280 g cold whole milk
  • 55 g sugar, 10 g salt, 10 g dried yeast
  • 280 g cold cultured butter, for laminating
  • 1 egg, beaten, to glaze

blocks.heading: Method
blocks.html:
1. Mix the dough, knead briefly and chill overnight.
  2. Beat the butter into a flat square between baking paper and chill.
  3. Enclose the butter in the dough and give it three single folds, chilling 30 minutes between each.
  4. Roll out, cut into triangles and roll each from the wide end.
  5. Prove for 2 hours until wobbly, glaze, and bake at 200°C for 18 minutes.

items.title: Our house flat white
items.seoDescription: How our baristas make the café’s favourite coffee.

blocks.headline: Our house flat white
blocks.body: A double ristretto and silky milk. The trick is the milk, not the machine.

image.alt: Milk being poured into a flat white

blocks.heading: Method
blocks.html:
1. Pull a double ristretto: 18 g of coffee, 30 g in the cup, about 25 seconds.
  2. Steam 150 ml of cold whole milk to 60°C, keeping the foam thin and glossy.
  3. Pour from close to the surface, then lift for the last third to finish the pattern.

Our beans come from Harbour Roasters, two streets away. Ask at the counter for a bag to take home.
